easy.q: President Chibota taught about the southern African greeting sawubona. What does it mean?
options: “Peace be with you”
“I see you”
“Welcome home”
easy.why: She said sawubona means “I see you.” It tells another person, “You matter.”

easy.q: Who thanked President Chibota and her husband, with tears in his eyes, because their daughter knew his name?
options: A school janitor
A school bus driver
A new neighbor
easy.why: A school janitor said their daughter greeted him, knew his name, and even helped him clean up after lunch.

easy.q: At the pool of Bethesda, many people had walked past a man for years. In this talk, what did the Savior do?
options: He asked His disciples to carry the man home
He told the man a parable about a lost sheep
He saw the man, ministered to him, and healed him
easy.why: President Chibota called this one of her favorite sawubona moments: the Savior “saw him, ministered to him, and healed him.”

easy.q: What did President Chibota plead with us to pray for?
options: To be noticed more often by other people
To see others as the Savior sees them
To have fewer hard days at school or work
easy.why: She pleaded with us as disciples of Jesus Christ “to pray to see others as He sees them and to treat them accordingly.”

easy.q: Which of these did President Chibota invite us to do this week?
options: Write a letter to a missionary we know
Memorize a favorite verse of scripture
Learn the name of someone who may feel unseen
easy.why: Her first invitation for the week was to learn the name of someone who may feel unseen. Knowing a name helps a person feel seen.

medium.q: Why did President Chibota mention the rich young man who walked away from the Savior sorrowing?
options: To explain why some people chose not to follow the Savior
To show that the Savior loved even one who would walk away
To teach that he later came back and became a disciple
To praise him for keeping the commandments from his youth
medium.why: She used him to show how the Savior truly saw people. Even of one who later walked away, the scriptures say, “Jesus beholding him loved him.”

medium.q: In this talk, what made the good Samaritan an example of choosing to see?
options: He kept the law more carefully than the other travelers did
He had more time and money to spare than the others
He already knew the injured man as a friend and neighbor
He saw a child of God in need instead of labels or differences
medium.why: President Chibota said that rather than letting labels or differences distract him, the good Samaritan “saw a child of God in need and acted.”

medium.q: According to President Chibota, how do we come to have our identity as sons and daughters of God?
options: We inherit it; it is not something we achieve
We earn it through years of faithful service
We receive it when we are called to serve
We find it by comparing ourselves with others
medium.why: She taught, “Our identity is not something we achieve; it is something we inherit as beloved sons and daughters of God.”

medium.q: When President Oaks told President Chibota, “You’ve been called for who you are,” what was she reminded of?
options: Callings come only to those who already feel ready
Feeling inadequate is a sign that our faith is weak
God’s view of us is more complete and more hopeful than our own
Church leaders see our weaknesses better than we do
medium.why: She said that in that moment she was reminded that “God’s view of us is always more complete and more hopeful than our own,” and it eased her feelings of inadequacy.

medium.q: What did President Chibota learn after praying to know how to help a coworker who seemed isolated?
options: Friendships grow best when we wait for others to reach out first
Large acts of service matter more than small, simple ones
People who seem isolated usually prefer to be left alone
Heavenly Father guides us to those who feel unseen when we ask
medium.why: As she acted on simple promptings to include him, their friendship grew. She learned that Heavenly Father “guides us to those who feel unseen.”

hard.q: Which everyday act best fits what President Chibota said the greeting sawubona communicates?
options: Calling a quick hello to everyone you pass in the hall
Stopping to greet a new classmate by name and listen to her
Greeting warmly the friends who always greet you first
Praising a classmate who has just won a school award
hard.why: She said sawubona is “an acknowledgment of another person’s worth and humanity.” It communicates, “I recognize you. I respect you. You matter.”

hard.q: President Chibota quoted the scripture that the Savior “calleth those things which be not as though they were.” What did she use it to teach?
options: He knows world events long before they take place
He asks us to speak only of pleasant and hopeful things
He sees not only who we are but who we can become
He calls people to serve who have never served before
hard.why: She used it to teach that the Savior sees our divine potential: “He sees not only who we are but who we can become.” His atoning sacrifice makes that potential possible.

hard.q: Someone sums up this talk by saying that learning to see others is only about them and changes nothing in us. What did President Chibota teach that corrects this?
options: Seeing others as children of God shapes how we see ourselves
Seeing ourselves clearly must come before we can see others
Seeing the labels others carry helps us understand our own
Seeing ourselves as others see us shows us who we truly are
hard.why: She taught, “Seeing others as children of God also influences the way we see ourselves,” even though the world invites us to focus on labels rather than eternal identity.

hard.q: What did President Chibota teach about the labels that may weigh heavily upon us?
options: They fade on their own once we stop thinking about them
We outgrow them as we accomplish more in life
They are accurate, but they last only for this life
Jesus Christ can raise us above them through His grace
hard.why: She testified that Jesus Christ can raise us above them: “His grace is sufficient to lift you above every label and limitation.”

hard.q: A youth makes a serious mistake and starts to feel that the mistake is all he or she is now. Which teaching from this talk answers that feeling most directly?
options: Labels help us when they push us to work harder
Our eternal identity does not change when we make mistakes
Mistakes are forgotten once other people stop noticing
A new label from the world can replace an old one
hard.why: President Chibota taught that our identity as spirit children of Heavenly Father “does not change when circumstances change, when we make mistakes, or when others misunderstand us.”
